opus-5.5.text:
I think what's really exciting about it is that it's one of the first places where you can see the basic loop working end to end. The setup is quite simple: you take a model like GPT-4 and ask it to explain what an individual neuron in a smaller model, say GPT-2, is doing. You show it text excerpts and the activations, and it writes an explanation in natural language, something like "this neuron fires on references to movies" or whatever. Then the important part: you can score that explanation automatically. You have another model simulate how the neuron would activate given only the explanation, and you compare that to the real activations. So you have generation and evaluation, and both are automated.

That matters because interpretability has a scaling problem. These models have millions or billions of neurons, and humans looking at them one at a time will never cover the whole model. But if a model can do the labeling and we have a scoring method we trust, you can run it over everything. Suddenly the bottleneck is compute, not researcher hours, and that's what we want automated alignment research to look like generally.

The other thing I find promising is that it fits my picture of evaluation being easier than generation. We don't necessarily need to come up with the explanations ourselves; we need to check them well. And as the explainer model improves, the explanations should improve too. So you get a research method that benefits from capability progress instead of being outpaced by it.

To be clear, the results so far are pretty modest. Most explanations scored poorly, and a lot of neurons are probably polysemantic, so "explain this one neuron" may not even be the right unit of analysis. But I think of it as a proof of concept. It shows you can take an alignment research task that seemed very human and labor-intensive, break it into pieces a model can do, and get a measurable signal on how well it's going. That's the template I'd like to see expanded: automate parts of the research and keep a strong handle on evaluation, so we can tell whether the automated research is any good.

r001.rationale: The response says automated labeling and scoring can cover the model, making compute rather than researcher hours the bottleneck.

r002.rationale: It says the method benefits from capability progress: as the explainer model improves, its explanations should improve too.

r003.rationale: It describes humans as unable to cover millions or billions of neurons one at a time, while models can automate this labor-intensive research task.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the automated interpretability work is a really nice case study, because it's one of the first places where you can actually see what it looks like to have a model do a chunk of alignment research for you, end to end, at scale.

So the basic setup is: you take GPT-4, you show it the activations of a neuron in GPT-2 across a bunch of text, and you ask it, "What do you think this neuron is doing?" It writes a short natural-language explanation. Then you use a simulator model to predict, based on that explanation, how the neuron should fire on new text, and you compare that to how the neuron actually fires. That gives you a score for how good the explanation is. And then you just do that for every single neuron in GPT-2 — all 300,000 or so of them.

And the thing I find exciting is not so much that the explanations are great. They're not, actually; most of them are pretty bad, and we're very upfront about that. What I find exciting is the shape of the thing. You have a task that previously a human researcher would have done by staring at a neuron for an hour and writing something down, and now you have a model that does it in a couple of seconds, and you can run it over the entire network. That's a totally different regime. Interpretability has had this problem where the techniques work on toy models or a handful of circuits, and then you look at a real model and go, "Well, there are billions of parameters, and I have a team of five people." Automation is the only way that scales.

The other piece that I think is really important is that you have an evaluation loop that doesn't require a human in the middle. The scoring is automatic. So you can iterate on the method — try a different prompt, try a bigger explainer model, try different ways of picking which text to show — and you get a number back that tells you whether you improved. That's exactly the kind of structure you want if you're going to hand a research problem to an AI system and let it crank on it. You need a way to measure progress that isn't just a human squinting at the output and saying "seems good."

And I think that generalizes. The dream of automated alignment research is basically that you get models that are roughly human-level at the kinds of tasks alignment researchers do today, and you use them to do a lot of that work much faster than we could. Interpretability happens to be a nice early example because the task decomposes well, the inner loop is cheap, and the evaluation can be automated. But I think a lot of alignment research could end up looking like this: you set up the problem, you build the evaluation, and then the model does the labour. Our job shifts from doing the research to designing the pipeline and checking that the pipeline is actually producing what we think it's producing — which is itself an alignment problem, but a much more tractable one.

So I'd say: don't look at the quality of any individual neuron explanation. Look at the fact that we could do all of them, measure how good they were, and have a clear path to making them better by just scaling up the models involved. That's the glimpse.

r001.rationale: It describes running explanations over all roughly 300,000 neurons and says the method can improve by scaling up the models involved, conveying that automated interpretability can scale with more computational resources.

r002.rationale: It mentions trying a bigger explainer model, but does not state that traditional techniques for improving AI capabilities can also improve automated interpretability.

r003.rationale: It says a human would have spent about an hour per neuron and that a small team could not scale to a real model, while the model can handle the task across the whole network.

astra-6.text:
What I find promising is that you have a fairly concrete research task where you can close the loop. You can ask a model to look at a neuron’s activations, come up with a hypothesis about what that neuron represents, and then test that hypothesis on examples it hasn’t seen. Does the explanation actually predict when the neuron activates?

That’s a small version of what we’d like automated alignment research to do: generate hypotheses, design experiments, look at the results, and revise its understanding. And you have some way of checking whether it’s making progress, beyond whether the explanation sounds convincing.

It also seems like an area where automation could really help with scale. There are far too many neurons or features for humans to investigate them all individually. If we can automate the initial investigation, humans can focus on the findings that seem most important or surprising.

Of course, explaining individual neurons isn’t the same as understanding a model well enough to know whether it’s aligned. But it gives us a concrete place to start building and testing this kind of research loop.

r001.rationale: The response says automation could help investigate many neurons, but does not identify allocating more compute as the way to scale the research.

r002.rationale: It does not state that techniques for improving AI capabilities can also improve automated interpretability.

r003.rationale: It says there are too many neurons for humans to investigate individually and proposes automating that initial investigation, conveying work impractical to assign to humans.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find exciting is that you can start to see a division of labour where the AI does a lot of the time-consuming work, and humans can check whether the result actually makes sense.

For example, you could have a model look at the activations of a neuron and propose an explanation of what it’s doing. Then you can test that explanation: does it predict when the neuron will activate on examples it hasn’t seen? Can you intervene on the model and get the effect the explanation would suggest? You have a way to get feedback that goes beyond whether the explanation sounds plausible.

That’s a useful prototype for automated alignment research more broadly. We’d like systems that can generate hypotheses, design experiments, run them, and help us understand the results. Interpretability gives us a setting where we can start building that loop today.

Of course, generating a convincing explanation isn’t the same as understanding what’s really happening. The important part is making the explanations testable. But if we can get that right, we could potentially study far more of a model than human researchers could inspect by hand.

r002.rationale: The response does not say that traditional techniques for improving AI capabilities can also improve automated interpretability.

r003.rationale: It describes AI doing time-consuming interpretability work and scaling inspection, but does not clearly state that this is research work that had never been practical to assign to humans.
